aaa: A test structure: prepare (arrange), perform the action (act), check the result (assert).
abc: A base class that cannot be instantiated and forces subclasses to implement certain methods (marked with `@abstractmethod`).
abstraction: Showing only what is essential and hiding the details. You drive a car with a wheel and pedals without knowing how the engine works.
access_control: The rules and checks that decide who can see or change which data and features.
accessibility: Making apps usable by everyone, including people using keyboards, screen readers or with visual impairments.
acid: Four transaction guarantees: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (no interference), Durability (committed data survives crashes).
adapter: A wrapper that converts one interface into another that your code expects, like a travel plug adapter.
adjacency_list: A graph representation where each node maps to a list of its neighbors: `{"A": ["B", "C"]}`.
aggregate: A function that summarizes many rows into one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.
amortized: The average cost per operation over a long sequence, when rare expensive operations are balanced by many cheap ones.
api: Application Programming Interface: the set of operations a system exposes for other programs, and the format to use them. A web API is used over HTTP.
api_gateway: A single entry point in front of backend services that handles routing, authentication, rate limiting and TLS.
array: Items stored next to each other in memory, accessed by index in O(1). A Python list is a dynamic array that grows automatically.
arrow_function: Short JS function syntax: `x => x * 2`. It does not have its own `this`.
assertion: A statement in a test that checks a condition; if it is false, the test fails.
asymmetric: Uses a key pair: a public key (shareable) and a private key (secret). Used for key exchange and digital signatures (RSA, ECDSA).
async_await: `async def` defines a function that can pause. `await` pauses it until a slow operation finishes, letting other tasks run meanwhile.
attribute: A value stored on an object and accessed with a dot: `user.name`. Methods are attributes too.
authn: Verifying who a user or system is (password, token, MFA).
authz: Deciding what an authenticated user is allowed to do or access.
autoscaling: Automatically adding or removing instances or Pods based on load.
autospec: An option for mocks to copy the real object's method signatures, so invalid calls fail in tests.
availability: The share of time a system is up and answering requests, often written as 'nines' (99.9%).
availability_zone: An isolated data center (or group) within a cloud region, with independent power and network.
b_agile: A way of building software in short iterations with frequent feedback, valuing working software and responding to change over rigid plans.
b_dod: A team-wide checklist of quality conditions that every work item must meet to count as complete.
b_kanban: A visual board method with limits on work in progress and continuous flow, instead of fixed sprints.
b_retro: A regular, blameless team meeting to review how the team worked and agree on concrete improvements.
b_scrum: An Agile framework with fixed sprints, three roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers) and events (planning, daily, review, retrospective).
b_sprint: A fixed period (1 to 4 weeks) in Scrum after which the team delivers a usable increment.
b_story_points: Story points are relative effort estimates; velocity is the number of points a team completes per sprint, used for forecasting.
b_tree: The balanced tree structure most database indexes use. It keeps values sorted so lookups, ranges and sorting take about log(n) steps.
b_user_story: A short description of a need from the user's view: "As a ..., I want ..., so that ...", with acceptance criteria to confirm it is done.
background_job: Work that runs outside the request/response cycle, in a separate worker process, e.g. sending emails or building reports.
backtracking: Exploring all candidate solutions by making a choice, recursing, then undoing the choice and trying the next one.
base_case: The simplest input of a recursive function, answered directly without another recursive call. It stops the recursion.
bfs: Exploring a graph level by level using a queue: all nodes 1 step away, then 2 steps, etc. Finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
big_o: A way to describe how an algorithm's time or memory grows as the input size n grows, ignoring constants: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²).
binary_search: Finding an item in a SORTED list by repeatedly checking the middle and discarding half. O(log n).
bit_manipulation: Working directly with the binary digits of numbers using operators like & (and), | (or), ^ (xor), << and >> (shifts).
blocking: A call that makes the thread wait and do nothing else until it finishes, like `time.sleep()` or `requests.get()`. Inside async code it freezes everything.
blue_green: Two identical environments; deploy to the idle one, then switch all traffic to it at once. Easy rollback.
box_model: Every element is a box made of content, padding, border and margin. `box-sizing` decides whether width includes padding and border.
broker: The server software that receives, stores and delivers messages between services (RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS).
brute_force: Trying huge numbers of possible passwords or keys until one works.
bst: A tree where each node has up to two children, all smaller keys on the left and bigger keys on the right. Fast search if balanced.
builder: A pattern that constructs a complex object step by step: `Request().url(u).header(h).timeout(5).build()`.
cache: A fast storage layer (usually memory) holding copies of data that is expensive to fetch or compute.
cache_aside: The app checks the cache first; on a miss it loads from the database and saves the result in the cache.
cache_stampede: Many requests miss the cache at the same moment (often when a hot key expires) and all hit the database together.
call_stack: The memory area that keeps track of active function calls. Each call adds a frame; returning removes it. Too many nested calls → stack overflow / RecursionError.
callback: A function you pass to other code so it can call it later, e.g. when a click happens or data arrives.
canary: Sending a small percentage of traffic to a new version first, watching metrics, then increasing gradually.
cap: In a distributed system, during a network partition you must choose between Consistency (everyone sees the latest data) and Availability (every request gets an answer).
cd: Automating the release process so changes can go (Delivery, with approval) or do go (Deployment, automatically) to production.
cdn: Content Delivery Network: servers around the world that cache static content close to users.
certificate: A digital document, signed by a trusted authority, that proves a public key belongs to a specific domain.
ci: Automatically building and testing every code change pushed to the shared repository.
circuit_breaker: A pattern that stops calling a failing service for a while after repeated errors, failing fast instead of waiting for timeouts.
class: A blueprint that defines what data (attributes) and behavior (methods) its objects have.
client_server: Clients (browsers, apps) send requests over the network; servers process them and send responses.
closure: A function that remembers variables from the place where it was created, even after that outer function has finished. It remembers the variable itself, not a frozen copy of its value.
cloud: Renting computing resources and managed services from a provider (AWS, Azure, GCP) on demand over the internet.
code_smell: A sign in the code that suggests a deeper design problem: huge classes, long functions, duplicated logic, too many parameters.
coercion: Automatic conversion of a value from one type to another, e.g. JavaScript turning "5" into 5 when comparing with ==.
cohesion: How closely the parts inside a module belong together. High cohesion = a focused module with one clear purpose.
collision: When two different keys produce the same slot in a hash table. Handled by chaining or probing; too many slow things down.
component: A reusable, self-contained piece of UI. In React, a function that receives props and returns JSX.
composite_index: An index on several columns in a specific order, e.g. (last_name, first_name). Useful only when queries filter on its leftmost columns.
composition: Building an object from other objects it holds as attributes ('has-a'): a Car has an Engine.
concurrency: Concurrency: handling several tasks in overlapping time by switching between them (one cook, many pots). Parallelism: literally running at the same instant on several CPU cores (many cooks).
conftest: A pytest file whose fixtures are automatically available to all tests in its folder and subfolders.
connection_pool: A set of already-open database connections that the app borrows and returns, instead of opening a new one for each query.
consistency: Every read sees the most recent write, no matter which server answers.
consistent_hashing: A way to assign keys to servers on a 'ring' so that adding or removing a server moves only a small fraction of keys.
container: A lightweight, isolated process packaged with its app and dependencies, sharing the host's operating system kernel.
context_manager: An object used with `with` that runs setup code at the start and cleanup code at the end, even if an error occurs. Files, locks and DB transactions use it.
contract_test: A test that checks a service's API still matches what its consumers expect.
controlled_input: A form input whose value comes from React state and is updated through onChange.
cookie: A small piece of data a server asks the browser to store and send back automatically on every request to that site. Often used for sessions.
core_web_vitals: Google's user-experience metrics: LCP (loading), INP (responsiveness), CLS (visual stability).
coroutine: The object created by calling an `async def` function. It is a pausable piece of work that only runs when awaited or scheduled.
cors: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: headers by which a server tells browsers which other websites (origins) may read its responses.
coupling: How much one module depends on the internals of another. Low coupling = you can change one without breaking the other.
coverage: The percentage of code lines or branches executed by the test suite.
cpu_bound: Work that spends its time calculating (image processing, math loops, compression). It is limited by processor speed, not by waiting.
cqrs: Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate models (and often stores) for writing data and for reading it.
credential_stuffing: Automatically trying username/password pairs leaked from other sites, exploiting password reuse.
csp: An HTTP header listing which sources the browser may load scripts, styles and other content from.
csrf: A malicious site makes the victim's browser send a request to another site where they are logged in, using their cookies.
css: Cascading Style Sheets: rules that control how HTML looks (colors, fonts, spacing, layout).
cve: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a public ID (e.g. CVE-2024-1234) for a known security flaw in software.
d_abstract_factory: A pattern with an interface that creates families of related objects without naming their concrete classes.
d_chain: A request passes through a sequence of handlers; each may process it or pass it on. Servlet filters work this way.
d_composite: A tree structure where individual items and groups share one interface, like files and folders.
d_covering_index: An index containing all columns a query needs, so the database can answer without reading the table.
d_cte: A named temporary result defined with `WITH` that makes complex queries easier to read; can be recursive.
d_dao: A class that hides how a particular table or entity is stored and retrieved, usually with CRUD methods.
d_ddl_dml: DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) defines structure. DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) changes data.
d_decorator: A wrapper with the same interface as the wrapped object that adds behavior, such as `BufferedReader` wrapping `FileReader`.
d_enum_singleton: Implementing a Singleton as a single-value Java enum; the JVM guarantees exactly one instance and it is thread-safe.
d_exists: A SQL test that is true if a subquery returns at least one row (EXISTS) or none (NOT EXISTS).
d_flyweight: Saves memory by sharing identical immutable objects, like the Integer cache and the string pool.
d_god_object: An anti-pattern: one huge class that knows and does too much. Split it by responsibility.
d_gof: The four authors of the book "Design Patterns" (1994), which catalogued 23 classic object-oriented design patterns.
d_junction: A table with two foreign keys that links two tables in a many-to-many relationship.
d_mvc: Model-View-Controller: separates data and rules (model), presentation (view) and request handling (controller).
d_normal_forms: Progressive rules for table design that remove redundancy: atomic values (1NF), full dependence on the key (2NF), no dependence between non-key columns (3NF).
d_proxy: An object that stands in for another with the same interface to control access or add behavior (transactions, caching, lazy loading).
d_relational: A database that stores data in tables with rows and columns, linked by keys, and queried with SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server).
d_surrogate_key: An artificial identifier (auto-increment id or UUID) with no business meaning, used as a stable primary key.
d_template_method: A base class fixes the steps of an algorithm and lets subclasses supply specific steps.
d_view: A named, saved query that behaves like a virtual table. A materialized view stores its result physically.
dag: Directed Acyclic Graph: a graph with one-way edges and no cycles. Dependency graphs are DAGs.
dataclass: A class decorated with `@dataclass` that automatically gets `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` from its declared fields. Great for plain data objects.
deadlock: Two or more transactions each wait for a lock the other holds, so none can continue. The database aborts one of them.
debounce: Delaying a function until events stop for a given time, so it runs once after a burst (e.g. typing).
decorator: A function that takes another function and returns a modified version of it. `@timer` above `def f` means `f = timer(f)`. Used for logging, caching, permissions, retries.
deep_copy: A completely independent copy, including copies of all nested objects: `copy.deepcopy(a)`.
default_arg: A value used when the caller does not pass that parameter: `def f(x=10)`. In Python it is created once, when the function is defined.
defer_async: Script attributes that download JS without blocking HTML parsing. defer keeps order and waits for parsing; async runs as soon as ready.
delivery_semantics: At-most-once (may lose messages), at-least-once (may duplicate), exactly-once (hard; usually achieved with idempotent processing).
denormalization: Intentionally duplicating some data to make reads faster, at the cost of more complex writes.
dependency: An external library your code needs, such as requests or Django. Versions are usually pinned in requirements.txt, pyproject.toml or a lock file.
dependency_injection: Giving an object the things it needs (database, API client, clock) from outside, usually via the constructor, instead of creating them inside.
deployment_k8s: An object that keeps a desired number of identical Pods running and handles rolling updates and rollbacks.
deque: 'Double-ended queue' from `collections`. Fast O(1) add/remove at both ends; ideal for queues.
descriptor: An object that customizes attribute access by defining `__get__`, `__set__` or `__delete__`. Properties and methods are built on it.
design_pattern: A named, proven solution to a recurring design problem (Factory, Strategy, Observer...). An idea to adapt, not a library.
deterministic: Always producing the same output for the same input, with no dependence on time, randomness or order.
dfs: Exploring a graph by going as deep as possible along one path before backtracking, using recursion or a stack.
dict: A collection of key → value pairs with fast lookup by key: `{"name": "Ana"}`. Keys must be hashable.
dijkstra: Finds the shortest path from one node to all others in a graph with non-negative edge weights, using a min-heap.
dip: High-level business code should depend on abstractions (interfaces), not on concrete low-level details.
dns: Domain Name System: translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses.
docker_compose: A tool to define and run several containers together from one YAML file.
docker_image: A read-only, layered template containing an app and everything it needs to run. Containers are started from images.
dockerfile: A text file with instructions (FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD...) that Docker follows to build an image.
dom: Document Object Model: the tree of objects the browser builds from HTML. JavaScript reads and changes it to update the page.
dp: Solving a problem by breaking it into overlapping subproblems and storing each subproblem's answer so it is computed only once.
duck_typing: 'If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck.' Code cares about what an object can do (its methods), not its class.
dunder: 'Double underscore' methods like `__init__`, `__eq__`, `__len__`. Python calls them automatically for built-in behavior (creation, comparison, len(), printing).
e2e_test: A test that exercises the whole system from the user's point of view, e.g. a browser clicking through the app.
edge_case: An unusual or extreme input at the boundary of what a function handles: empty, zero, max size, None.
encapsulation: Keeping data and the methods that use it together and hiding internal details, so other code uses only a safe public interface.
encoding: Encoding (base64, UTF-8) only changes the representation; anyone can reverse it. Encryption needs a key to read the data.
encryption: Scrambling data so only someone with the right key can read it. Reversible with the key, unlike hashing.
endpoint: One specific URL + HTTP method your API handles, e.g. `GET /users/{id}`, usually mapped to one function.
env_var: A named value provided to a program by its environment (`os.environ["KEY"]`), commonly used for configuration and secrets.
etag: A version identifier for a resource sent by the server. Lets clients ask 'has it changed?' and get 304 Not Modified if not.
event_bubbling: An event on an element also triggers on its parent, then its parent's parent, up to the document.
event_delegation: Handling events of many child elements with one listener on their common parent, thanks to bubbling.
event_loop: The engine of asyncio. It runs many tasks in one thread, switching to another task whenever the current one is waiting (at an `await`).
event_loop_js: The mechanism that runs JS on a single thread: run synchronous code, then all microtasks (promises), then the next macrotask (timers, events).
eventual_consistency: Copies of data may differ for a short time after a write, but will all become the same if no new writes arrive.
exception: An error object raised while the program runs (ValueError, KeyError...). If nobody catches it with try/except, the program stops and shows a traceback.
exit_code: A number a process returns when it ends: 0 means success, anything else means an error or a signal.
explain: A SQL command that shows how the database plans to run a query (indexes used, scans, joins). EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs it and shows real timings.
f_array_methods: Array methods that return new results: map transforms each item, filter keeps matching items, reduce combines items into one value.
f_bundler: A build tool that transpiles, combines and minifies source files into optimized files for the browser, with a hot-reload dev server.
f_context: A way to make a value available to all descendant components without passing props at every level.
f_npm: npm is the Node package manager. `package.json` lists metadata, scripts and dependencies; `npm install` downloads them to `node_modules`.
f_rtl: A library that renders React components in tests and queries them like a user would (by role or text).
f_spa: A web app that loads once and updates the view with JavaScript and API calls instead of full page reloads.
facade: A simple front-door class that hides a complicated subsystem behind a few easy methods.
factory: A function or class whose job is to create objects, choosing the right concrete type: `create_parser("json")` returns a JsonParser.
failover: Automatically switching to a backup component when the main one fails.
fake: A simple working implementation used in tests instead of the real one, e.g. an in-memory database.
feature_flag: A configuration switch that turns a feature on or off at runtime, for all users or some, without redeploying.
fixture: A function that prepares something a test needs (data, connection, client) and optionally cleans it up afterwards.
flaky_test: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any code change.
flexbox: A CSS layout model for arranging items in one direction (row or column), with easy alignment and spacing.
foreign_key: A column that holds the primary key of a row in another table, creating a relationship the database can enforce.
function: A named, reusable block of code. It receives inputs (parameters), does something, and can give back a result with `return`.
garbage_collector: The part of a language runtime that automatically frees memory no longer in use. In Python, the `gc` module mainly cleans up reference cycles.
generator: A function that uses `yield` to produce values one at a time, pausing between them. It does not build the whole result in memory, and it can only be consumed once.
generic: A type with a placeholder, like `list[T]`, so the same code works for many types while keeping type information.
gil: A lock inside CPython (the standard Python) that allows only one thread to run Python code at a time. It keeps Python's memory management simple and safe, but it means threads cannot do heavy calculations in parallel.
git_branch: An independent line of development in Git. Lets you work on a feature without touching the main code until it is merged.
git_commit: A saved snapshot of changes in a Git repository, with an ID and a message describing the change.
global_state: Data that any part of the program can read and change. It creates hidden connections between code and makes testing harder.
graph: A set of nodes (vertices) connected by edges. Edges can be directed or undirected, weighted or not.
graphql: An API query language where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs in one request, through a single endpoint.
grid: A CSS layout model for arranging items in rows and columns at the same time.
group_by: Groups rows that share a value so aggregate functions can be computed per group.
grpc: A high-performance RPC framework using Protobuf binary messages over HTTP/2, with code generated from a shared schema.
hash: A number calculated from a value, used to find it quickly in sets and dict keys. Equal values must have equal hashes. Only immutable values are normally hashable.
hash_table: A structure that stores key → value pairs in an array, using a hash of the key to find the slot. Python's dict and set. O(1) average lookup.
hashing: A one-way function that maps any input to a fixed-size fingerprint. The same input always gives the same output.
header: A name: value pair carrying extra information with a request or response, e.g. `Authorization: Bearer <token>` or `Content-Type: application/json`.
heap: A tree-based structure that always gives quick access to the smallest (min-heap) or largest item. Python: `heapq`. Push/pop O(log n).
high_availability: Designing a system to keep working despite failures, using redundancy and automatic failover.
higher_order: A function that receives functions as arguments or returns a function. Decorators, `map` and `sorted(key=...)` are examples.
hmac: A signature computed from a message and a secret key. Anyone with the key can verify that the message is authentic and unchanged.
hoisting: JavaScript's behavior of moving declarations to the top of their scope before running code.
hook: Functions starting with `use` (useState, useEffect, useMemo...) that give function components state and lifecycle features.
horizontal_scaling: Adding more servers that share the work, usually behind a load balancer. Requires stateless app design.
hsts: HTTP Strict Transport Security: a header telling browsers to always use HTTPS for a domain.
html: HyperText Markup Language: the tags that define a web page's structure and content (headings, paragraphs, links, forms).
http: The protocol browsers and apps use to talk to web servers: a client sends a request (method, URL, headers, body) and gets a response (status code, headers, body).
http2: A newer version of HTTP that sends many requests at once over one connection and compresses headers.
http_method: The verb of a request: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove).
httponly: A cookie flag that hides the cookie from JavaScript, so injected scripts cannot steal it.
https: HTTP running inside an encrypted TLS connection. Protects data from being read or changed and verifies the server's identity.
hydration: Attaching JavaScript behavior to server-rendered HTML in the browser so it becomes interactive.
iac: Defining servers, networks and databases in code files, so infrastructure is versioned, reviewed and reproducible.
iam: Identity and Access Management: the AWS (or other cloud) system for users, roles and permissions.
idempotent: An operation that has the same effect whether you do it once or many times. Setting x = 5 is idempotent; adding 1 to x is not.
identity: Which exact object in memory a variable refers to. `id(x)` shows it and `is` compares it. Two equal lists can still be two different objects.
idor: Insecure Direct Object Reference: accessing someone else's data by changing an ID in the request, because ownership is not checked.
immutable: An object that cannot change after creation, like int, str, tuple or frozenset. 'Changing' it really creates a new object.
immutable_infra: Replacing servers with freshly built images for every change instead of modifying them in place.
index: A sorted lookup structure on one or more columns that lets the database find rows quickly without scanning the whole table.
inheritance: A class (child) reuses and extends another class (parent): `class Dog(Animal)`. The child gets the parent's methods and can override them.
inner_join: Returns only rows that have a match in both tables.
input_validation: Checking that incoming data matches what is expected (type, length, format, range) and rejecting anything else.
instance: A concrete object created from a class. `rex = Dog()` makes `rex` an instance of Dog. The class is the blueprint; the instance is the house.
integration_test: A test that checks several real components working together, such as your code with a real database.
interface: The set of methods an object promises to offer, without saying how they work inside. In Python often expressed with an ABC or a Protocol.
io_bound: Work that spends most of its time waiting for input/output: network calls, disk reads, database queries. The CPU is mostly idle while waiting.
isolation_level: How much concurrent transactions are protected from each other: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable.
isp: Prefer several small, focused interfaces over one large one, so classes implement only what they use.
iterable: Anything you can loop over with `for`: lists, strings, dicts, files, ranges. Calling `iter()` on it gives an iterator.
iterator: An object that returns the next item each time you call `next()` on it, and remembers where it is. When it has no more items, it raises StopIteration.
j_abstract_class: A class that cannot be instantiated directly. It can hold fields, constructors and ready methods, plus `abstract` methods that subclasses must implement.
j_access_modifier: A keyword that controls who can see a class member: public (all), protected (package and subclasses), none (package only), private (same class only).
j_arraylist: A List backed by a resizable array: fast access by index, fast appends, compact memory. The default choice for lists.
j_atomic: `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicLong`... provide thread-safe operations such as `incrementAndGet()` without explicit locks.
j_autocloseable: An interface with one method, `close()`. Any class implementing it can be used in try-with-resources.
j_boxing: Automatic conversion between a primitive and its wrapper object (int to Integer and back). Unboxing a null wrapper throws NullPointerException.
j_bytecode: The intermediate, platform-neutral instructions that `javac` produces from your `.java` files (stored in `.class` files). The JVM runs it.
j_checked_exc: An exception the compiler forces you to catch or declare with `throws`, such as IOException.
j_cme: Thrown when a collection is structurally modified while an iterator is walking it (even in one thread). Use removeIf or Iterator.remove instead.
j_collections: Java's built-in set of data structures and interfaces: List, Set, Map, Queue, Deque and their implementations (ArrayList, HashSet, HashMap, ArrayDeque...).
j_comparable: An interface with `compareTo` that gives a class its single natural ordering.
j_comparator: A separate object with `compare(a, b)` defining a custom ordering, e.g. sort people by age or by name.
j_completable_future: A result that will be available later, with methods to chain steps (`thenApply`, `thenCompose`, `thenCombine`) without blocking.
j_concurrenthashmap: A thread-safe Map built for many threads at once, with non-blocking reads and fine-grained locking on writes. Offers atomic methods like `merge` and `computeIfAbsent`.
j_defensive_copy: Copying a mutable object when receiving it or returning it, so outsiders cannot change your internal state.
j_deserialization: Feeding crafted serialized data to an app so rebuilding the objects runs attacker-controlled code (gadget chains).
j_equals_hashcode: `equals` says whether two objects are logically the same. `hashCode` gives a number used by hash collections. If two objects are equal, they must return the same hashCode.
j_executor: The Java API to submit tasks to a thread pool and get a `Future` with the result.
j_final: A modifier that prevents change: a final variable is assigned once, a final method cannot be overridden, a final class cannot be extended.
j_finally: A block that runs after try/catch no matter what happened, including after a return or an exception. Typically used for cleanup.
j_gc: The JVM component that automatically frees objects that can no longer be reached, so developers do not call `free` manually.
j_generics: Parameterized types such as `List<String>` that let the compiler check element types and remove the need for casts.
j_hashmap: A Map that finds values by hashing the key into buckets. Average O(1) get and put. Not thread-safe; allows one null key.
j_heap: The shared memory area where all objects live. It is cleaned by the garbage collector. When it is full: OutOfMemoryError.
j_immutable_class: A class whose objects never change after construction (final fields, no setters). Safe to share between threads.
j_jdk: JRE (Java Runtime Environment) = JVM + standard libraries, enough to run programs. JDK (Java Development Kit) = JRE + developer tools such as the compiler `javac`.
j_jvm: The program that loads Java bytecode and executes it, manages memory (garbage collection) and optimizes hot code while running. Each operating system has its own JVM.
j_lambda: A short anonymous function written as `(args) -> expression`, e.g. `n -> n * 2`. It can be used wherever a functional interface is expected.
j_mem_leak: Objects that are still referenced (so the GC cannot free them) but will never be used again, causing the heap to grow.
j_optional: A container that may hold a value or be empty. Used as a return type to make "might be missing" explicit instead of returning null.
j_overload: Several methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class. The compiler chooses at compile time.
j_override: A subclass provides its own implementation of an inherited method with the same signature. The JVM chooses the version at runtime from the real object type.
j_primitive: A basic value type built into Java: int, long, double, boolean, char, byte, short, float. It is not an object and can never be null.
j_record: A compact immutable data class (Java 16+): `record Point(int x, int y) {}` generates constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString.
j_runtime_exc: An exception extending RuntimeException (NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException...). The compiler does not force you to handle it; it usually signals a bug.
j_stack_mem: A per-thread memory area holding one frame per active method call with its local variables. Too many nested calls cause StackOverflowError.
j_static: A class-level member: one copy shared by all objects, usable without creating an instance (`Math.max(1, 2)`).
j_stream: A way to process collections as a pipeline (filter, map, collect). Streams are lazy: nothing runs until a terminal operation such as `toList()` or `forEach` is called.
j_string_pool: A special memory area where Java keeps one copy of each string literal, so identical literals share the same object.
j_stringbuilder: A mutable text buffer for building strings efficiently. Unlike String, appending to it does not copy the whole text every time.
j_stw: A moment when the JVM pauses all application threads so the garbage collector can work safely. Long pauses cause latency spikes.
j_synchronized: A keyword that lets only one thread at a time run a block or method for a given lock object, and makes its changes visible to other threads.
j_thread_pool: A fixed or bounded group of reusable worker threads that execute queued tasks, avoiding the cost and risk of one thread per task.
j_try_with_res: A try statement that opens resources in parentheses and closes them automatically at the end, even after an exception.
j_type_erasure: The compiler removes generic type arguments after checking, so at runtime `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are both plain `List`.
j_virtual_thread: A lightweight thread (Java 21) scheduled by the JVM instead of the OS. Millions can exist, which suits I/O-heavy servers.
j_volatile: A field modifier guaranteeing that all threads see the latest written value. It does not make compound actions like `count++` atomic.
javascript: The programming language that runs in browsers (and on servers with Node.js) to make pages interactive.
join: Combining rows of two tables based on a related column, e.g. orders.customer_id = customers.id.
json: A text data format with objects `{"key": value}` and arrays `[...]`. The standard format for web APIs.
jwt: A compact token with three parts (header.payload.signature). The payload holds claims like user ID and expiry; the signature proves the server issued it.
k8s_secret: An object to hold sensitive values and inject them into Pods. Encoded, not encrypted, by default.
kadane: An O(n) algorithm for the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray: at each element, extend the current run or restart.
kafka: A distributed event streaming platform: messages are stored in an ordered, replayable log split into partitions.
keyword_arg: An argument passed by name: `f(size=10)`. Order does not matter and calls are easier to read.
kubernetes: A system that automates deploying, scaling, healing and networking containers across a cluster of machines.
lambda: A small anonymous function written in one expression: `lambda x: x * 2` is the same as `def f(x): return x * 2`.
latency: The time one operation takes from start to finish, e.g. how long a request waits for its response.
layer_cache: Docker reuses the result of each build step if its inputs did not change, which makes rebuilds fast.
lazy: Computing values only when they are actually needed, instead of all at once in advance. Saves memory and time when not everything is used.
leader_follower: One node (leader) accepts writes and copies them to followers, which serve reads and can replace the leader.
least_privilege: Giving every user, service and key only the minimum permissions it needs.
left_join: Returns all rows from the left table, plus matching rows from the right one (NULL where there is no match).
linear_search: Checking items one by one from the start until the target is found. O(n).
linked_list: A sequence of nodes where each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. Easy to insert/remove; slow to access by index.
list: An ordered, changeable collection: `[1, 2, 3]`. Items are accessed by position, starting at 0.
list_comprehension: A compact way to build a list from a loop: `[x * 2 for x in nums if x > 0]`. With parentheses instead of brackets it becomes a generator expression.
load_balancer: A component that spreads incoming requests across several servers and skips unhealthy ones.
load_test: Simulating many concurrent users to measure performance and find the system's limits.
lock: A tool that lets only one thread at a time run a protected piece of code: `with lock: ...`. Prevents race conditions.
logs: Logs: timestamped text events. Metrics: numeric measurements over time. Traces: the timed path of one request through services.
lru: A fixed-size cache that removes the Least Recently Used item when it needs space.
lsp: A subclass must work anywhere its parent class is expected, without surprising the caller.
media_query: A CSS condition (screen width, dark mode, etc.) that applies rules only when true.
memoization: Caching a function's results by its arguments, so repeated calls with the same input return instantly. Python: `@functools.lru_cache`.
merge: Combining the changes from one branch into another. Keeps both histories and adds a merge commit when needed.
merge_sort: A sort that splits the list in halves, sorts each, and merges them. Always O(n log n), stable, uses extra memory.
message_queue: A buffer where one service puts messages and another takes them later, so they don't have to be available at the same time.
metaclass: The 'class of a class': it creates classes the way classes create objects. The default is `type`. Rarely needed in everyday code.
metadata: Data about data. For a function: its name (`__name__`), docstring (`__doc__`), module, and so on.
method: A function defined inside a class. It receives the object (`self`) automatically as its first argument.
mfa: Multi-factor authentication: requiring two or more different kinds of proof of identity, such as a password plus a phone code.
microservices: An architecture where an application is split into small, independently deployable services that communicate over the network.
microtask: Microtasks (promise callbacks) run right after the current code, before any macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, UI events).
middleware: Code that runs around every request and response in a web app, for cross-cutting tasks like logging, auth, CORS or timing.
ml_ab_test: An online experiment that randomly splits users between two versions and compares a metric.
ml_accuracy: The share of predictions that are correct. It can mislead when one class is much more common than the other.
ml_bagging: Training many models on bootstrap samples (random samples with replacement) and averaging them. It lowers variance.
ml_bias_variance: Bias is error from a model that is too simple; variance is error from a model that is too sensitive to the training sample. Lowering one usually raises the other.
ml_calibration: How well predicted probabilities match real frequencies. A calibrated model is right about 70% of the time when it says 70%.
ml_class_imbalance: When one class is much rarer than the others, as with fraud. Accuracy becomes a poor metric.
ml_class_weight: Weights that make errors on a rare class count more in the loss, without changing the data.
ml_classification: A task where the model predicts a category, such as spam or not spam.
ml_clustering: An unsupervised task that groups similar items together. k-means is a common method.
ml_concept_drift: The relation between inputs and label changes, so what the model learned stops being true.
ml_confusion_matrix: A table that counts the true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives of a classifier.
ml_covariate_shift: The input distribution changes while the relation between inputs and label stays the same.
ml_cross_validation: Splitting the data into k folds and training k times, each time validating on a different fold, then averaging the scores.
ml_data_leakage: When information from outside the training data, such as the test set or the future, reaches the model during training. Scores look better than they will be in real use.
ml_decision_tree: A model that predicts by asking a series of yes/no questions about the features. A deep tree easily overfits.
ml_drift: A change over time in the data a model receives, or in the relation between inputs and outcome, that makes the model worse.
ml_ensemble: A model made by combining several models, usually to get better and more stable predictions.
ml_f1: The harmonic mean of precision and recall. It is low if either one is low.
ml_feature: An input variable the model uses to make a prediction, such as the size of a house.
ml_feature_scaling: Rescaling numeric features to a similar range, for example by standardization. Distance-based and penalized models need it; trees do not.
ml_feature_selection: Choosing which features to keep. It is part of training, so it must be done inside cross-validation.
ml_gradient_boosting: An ensemble built step by step: each new small tree is trained to reduce the errors of the ones before it.
ml_group_kfold: Cross-validation that keeps all rows of the same group (patient, user, device) in the same fold.
ml_hyperparameter: A setting chosen before training, such as the learning rate or the maximum depth of a tree. It is tuned by trying values, not learned.
ml_l1: Penalizes the sum of absolute coefficient values. It can set coefficients to exactly zero.
ml_l2: Penalizes the sum of squared coefficient values. It shrinks coefficients without usually making them zero.
ml_label: The value the model must predict, such as the price of a house or whether an email is spam.
ml_nested_cv: Cross-validation with a second, inner cross-validation used to tune hyperparameters, so the outer score stays honest.
ml_overfitting: When a model learns the noise and details of the training data, so it scores well on training data and badly on new data.
ml_parameter: A value the model learns from the training data, such as a weight in a linear model.
ml_permutation_importance: A way to measure the value of a feature: shuffle it on held-out data and see how much the score drops.
ml_pr_auc: A curve of precision against recall. Its area (average precision) is more informative than ROC-AUC when positives are rare.
ml_precision: Of the cases the model flagged as positive, the share that really are positive: TP / (TP + FP).
ml_random_forest: An ensemble of decision trees trained on random samples of rows and features, whose votes are averaged to lower variance.
ml_recall: Of the real positive cases, the share the model found: TP / (TP + FN).
ml_regression: A task where the model predicts a number on a continuous scale, such as a price or a time.
ml_regularization: A penalty on model complexity added during training to reduce overfitting.
ml_roc_auc: The area under the ROC curve (recall against false positive rate). It equals the chance that a random positive is scored above a random negative; 0.5 is a random ranking.
ml_selection_bias: When the training data is not representative because of how it was collected, for example only the outcomes of approved loans.
ml_stratified: A split that keeps the same class proportions in every part.
ml_supervised: Learning from examples that come with the right answer (labels).
ml_target_leakage: A feature that contains the answer, usually because its value is only known after the outcome happened.
ml_threshold: The probability above which a classifier predicts the positive class. Moving it trades precision for recall.
ml_time_series_split: A split where training data always comes before validation data in time, as in real forecasting.
ml_train_test_split: Dividing the data into a part to train the model and a part kept aside to measure how it does on unseen data.
ml_training_serving_skew: A difference between the data or the feature code used in training and in production.
ml_underfitting: When a model is too simple to capture the pattern, so it does badly even on the training data.
ml_unsupervised: Looking for structure in data that has no labels, such as groups of similar customers.
ml_validation_set: Data used to compare models and tune hyperparameters, kept separate from the final test set.
mock: A test double that replaces a real dependency, returns what you configure, and records calls so you can verify them.
monolith: An application built and deployed as a single unit. Can be well organized internally (modular monolith).
monotonic_stack: A stack kept in increasing or decreasing order, used to find the next greater or smaller element for every item in O(n).
mro: The order in which Python searches classes for a method or attribute when inheritance is involved. See it with `ClassName.__mro__`.
multi_stage: A Dockerfile with several FROM stages, where later stages copy only the needed outputs from earlier ones.
multiple_inheritance: A class with more than one parent: `class D(B, C)`. Python resolves conflicts using the MRO.
mutable: An object that can be changed after it is created, like a list, dict or set. If two variables point to the same mutable object, a change through one is visible through the other.
mutation_testing: Planting small bugs in the code to check whether the test suite notices them.
n_aes: Advanced Encryption Standard: the standard symmetric cipher. One key encrypts and decrypts. Used by TLS, disk encryption and cloud storage.
n_aks: Azure Kubernetes Service: Microsoft's managed Kubernetes. Azure runs the control plane for you.
n_alb_nlb: AWS load balancers. ALB works at layer 7 (HTTP) and can route by path or host. NLB works at layer 4 (TCP/UDP) for very high speed.
n_app_props: Spring Boot's main config file: server port, database URL and any custom settings. Profiles can override it for each environment.
n_arraydeque: A fast resizable-array deque in Java. It is the usual choice for a stack or a queue instead of `Stack` or `LinkedList`.
n_assignment: `age = 30` creates the name `age` and makes it refer to the value 30. Python variables are labels attached to objects, not boxes that hold values.
n_autowired: Asks Spring to inject a dependency. Prefer constructor injection; with a single constructor `@Autowired` is optional.
n_aws: Amazon's cloud platform: rentable servers (EC2), storage (S3), databases (RDS), networking (VPC) and hundreds of other services, billed by usage.
n_b_ambiguity: Ask clarifying questions, state your assumptions, split the work into small steps, ship something early and iterate with feedback.
n_b_career: Answer with growth in skills and responsibility (deeper technical expertise, leading small projects) that fits what the company offers. Be honest, not rehearsed.
n_b_comm: Start from the goal and the impact, avoid jargon, use an analogy or example, and check understanding. Say what you need from them.
n_b_conflict: Listen first, find the shared goal, separate the problem from the person, bring data, agree on a next step. Show respect and a calm result, not who won.
n_b_deadline: Clarify what is urgent versus important, agree on scope with the stakeholders, deliver the most valuable part first, communicate risks early and say no to the rest.
n_b_failure: Pick a real mistake, own it without blaming others, explain what you changed afterward (a test, a checklist, a process) and what you learned.
n_b_feedback: Listen without defending, ask questions to understand, thank the person, act on it and show the change. Interviewers look for a growth mindset.
n_b_impact: Close a story with a result and, if you can, a number: time saved, errors reduced, users helped. It turns 'I worked on it' into 'it mattered'.
n_b_learning: Show a method: official docs, a small prototype, asking someone experienced, then applying it to real work. Give the result and how fast you got there.
n_b_mentoring: Helping someone grow: explain the why, give small tasks with feedback, pair on problems and let them own the solution. Describe how they improved.
n_b_motivation: Connect your goals to the role and the company: what you want to learn, what you can contribute and something specific you researched about their product or team.
n_b_ownership: Showing that you took responsibility beyond your task: you saw the problem, acted, followed through and owned the result. Use 'I', not only 'we'.
n_b_questions: Ask about the team, how work is planned and reviewed, onboarding, what success looks like in 6 months and the main technical challenges. Avoid only asking about salary or perks.
n_b_strengths: Strengths: pick 2 or 3 relevant ones with a short example. Weakness: a real one that is not critical for the job, plus what you do to improve it.
n_b_teamwork: Working well with others: share information, help teammates, give and accept review comments, respect different views and keep a positive attitude under pressure.
n_b_tellme: A simple structure for 'Tell me about yourself': what you do now, how you got here (1 or 2 key steps), and why this role is next. About 1 to 2 minutes.
n_bitwise: `&` AND, `|` OR, `^` XOR, `<<` and `>>` shift bits. `n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, so it is 0 only for powers of two.
n_box_sizing: With `border-box`, `width` includes padding and border, so a 200px box stays 200px. With the default `content-box`, padding and border are added on top.
n_builtin_exc: ValueError: right type, bad value. TypeError: wrong type. KeyError: missing dictionary key. IndexError: index out of range.
n_cacheable: Caches the result of a method by its arguments. The next call with the same arguments returns the cached value without running the method.
n_class_file: A compiled Java file that contains bytecode. The JVM loads and runs it on any operating system.
n_cls: A Core Web Vitals metric that measures how much the page layout jumps while it loads. Lower is better.
n_command_pattern: Wraps a request as an object, so it can be queued, logged, retried or undone. Natural fit for undo/redo and job queues.
n_content_type: A header that says what format the body has, such as `application/json`.
n_count: `COUNT(*)` counts all rows. `COUNT(column)` counts only rows where that column is NOT NULL.
n_cpu: Central Processing Unit: the chip that runs program instructions. 'CPU-bound' work is limited by how fast the chip can calculate.
n_demeter: 'Talk only to your immediate friends.' A method should not reach through a chain of objects (`a.b.c.d()`); chains couple your code to the inner structure of other classes.
n_dict_order: Since Python 3.7 a dict keeps keys in the order they were inserted, and the language guarantees it (it was only a CPython detail in 3.6).
n_distinct: Removes duplicate rows from the result: `SELECT DISTINCT country FROM users` returns each country once.
n_dry: Don't Repeat Yourself: each piece of knowledge should live in one place, so a change needs only one edit.
n_dynamic_array: An array that doubles its capacity when full (Python list, Java ArrayList). One append is occasionally O(n), but the amortized cost is O(1).
n_ebs: Elastic Block Store: network disks for EC2 instances. The data stays when the instance stops, like a virtual hard drive.
n_ecr_acr: Managed container registries: Amazon Elastic Container Registry and Azure Container Registry. They store your Docker images privately.
n_enter_exit: The two methods that make an object a context manager for `with`. `__enter__` runs at the start; `__exit__` always runs at the end, even after an error.
n_entity: Marks a class as a JPA entity: Hibernate maps it to a database table and its fields to columns.
n_entitygraph: Ways to load an entity together with its relations in a single query, which fixes the N+1 problem.
n_eq_hash: `__eq__` defines `==`. If you define it, also define `__hash__` consistently (equal objects must have equal hashes) or the object misbehaves in sets and as dict keys.
n_equality: `==` converts types before comparing (`0 == ""` is true). `===` compares value AND type without converting (`0 === ""` is false). Prefer `===`.
n_fetch: The browser API for HTTP requests. It returns a Promise, does NOT throw on 404 or 500 (check `res.ok`), and `res.json()` is also async.
n_fifo_lifo: FIFO: first in, first out, like a queue at a shop. LIFO: last in, first out, like a stack of plates.
n_floor_div: In Python 3, `/` always gives a float (`7 / 2` is `3.5`). `//` is floor division and rounds down (`7 // 2` is `3`). `%` gives the remainder (`7 % 2` is `1`).
n_floyd: Two pointers move through a linked list, one step and two steps at a time. If there is a cycle they meet; if not, the fast one reaches the end. Uses O(1) extra space.
n_g1_zgc: Modern JVM garbage collectors. G1 is the default: it works in regions and aims at predictable pauses. ZGC aims at pauses of a few milliseconds even on huge heaps.
n_gather: Runs several coroutines concurrently and waits for all of them, returning their results in order.
n_gcp: Google's cloud platform. It offers equivalents of the AWS and Azure services: Compute Engine (virtual machines), Cloud Storage (object storage) and GKE (managed Kubernetes).
n_git_cmds: `add` stages changes, `commit` saves a snapshot locally, `push` uploads commits to the remote, `pull` downloads and merges remote commits.
n_hashset: A Java Set backed by a hash table: no duplicates, no order, average O(1) add and contains. It needs correct `equals` and `hashCode`.
n_hpa: A Kubernetes object that changes the number of Pod replicas based on CPU or custom metrics.
n_init: The initializer method that runs when a new object is created. It sets the starting attributes: `def __init__(self, name): self.name = name`.
n_ip: A number that identifies a device on a network, like 192.168.1.10 (IPv4). DNS translates names into IP addresses.
n_iter_next: The iterator protocol. `__iter__` returns the iterator; `__next__` returns the next item and raises `StopIteration` when there are no more.
n_javac: `javac` compiles `.java` source into `.class` bytecode. `java` starts the JVM and runs that bytecode, or a whole JAR with `java -jar`.
n_jdbctemplate: A Spring helper that runs SQL through JDBC and removes the boilerplate: connections, statements and cleanup are handled for you.
n_jerrors: StackOverflowError: the call stack is full, usually from infinite or very deep recursion. OutOfMemoryError: the heap has no room left even after garbage collection.
n_jparepo: A Spring Data interface that gives ready-made CRUD, paging and sorting methods for an entity. You only declare the interface.
n_json_loads: `json.loads` turns a JSON string into Python objects. `json.dumps` turns Python objects into a JSON string.
n_jsx: A syntax that lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript (React). The build step compiles it into normal function calls.
n_latest_tag: Docker's default tag. It is only a name that moves, so it does not mean 'newest'. Pin an exact version in production.
n_lock_order: The standard way to avoid deadlocks: every transaction takes locks in the same global order, and keeps transactions short.
n_longadder: A Java counter built for many threads: it spreads updates over several cells and sums them on read, so it scales better than `AtomicLong` under contention.
n_lru_cache: A decorator that remembers the results of a function for the same arguments (memoization). Arguments must be hashable, so passing a list raises `TypeError`.
n_maven_layout: The standard layout: `src/main/java` (code), `src/main/resources` (config), `src/test/java` (tests). Build output goes to `target/`.
n_multiprocessing: Runs Python code in separate processes, each with its own interpreter and GIL, so CPU-bound work uses several cores. Cost: starting processes and pickling the data sent between them.
n_mvn_cmds: `clean` deletes `target/`, `test` runs the unit tests, `package` builds the JAR, `install` also copies it into `~/.m2`.
n_nist: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology. It publishes widely used security and cloud standards, such as the definition of cloud computing.
n_null_compare: NULL means 'unknown', so `= NULL` is never true. Use `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`.
n_oidc: A login layer on top of OAuth 2.0. It tells the app who the user is through an ID token (a JWT).
n_os: The software that manages the hardware and runs other programs (Linux, Windows, macOS). It gives programs files, memory, processes and networking.
n_override: Tells the compiler that this method must override one from a parent class or interface. If the signature does not match, compilation fails.
n_permutations: The number of ways to order n distinct items is n! (n factorial). Generating them all takes at least n! steps, which grows extremely fast.
n_pid: Process ID: the number the operating system gives to each running process. In a container, PID 1 is the main process; when it exits, the container stops.
n_plus_1: Running 1 query to get a list of N items, then 1 more query for each item. Fixed by loading related data in bulk (JOIN or IN query).
n_print_return: `print` shows a value on the screen and the function then returns `None`. `return` hands a value back to the caller so other code can use it, and it ends the function.
n_promise_all: Runs promises in parallel and resolves with all results, but rejects as soon as ONE rejects. `Promise.allSettled` waits for all and reports each outcome.
n_pyproject: The standard config file of a Python project: metadata, dependencies and tool settings in one place.
n_quic: A modern transport protocol built on UDP and used by HTTP/3. It sets up connections faster and avoids TCP head-of-line blocking.
n_ram: Random-access memory: fast, temporary memory where running programs keep their data. It is cleared when the program ends or the computer restarts.
n_rbac: Role-Based Access Control: permissions are given to roles (admin, editor, viewer) and users receive roles, instead of assigning permissions one by one.
n_resttemplate: Spring's classic HTTP client for calling other REST services. In newer code `RestClient` or `WebClient` is preferred.
n_retry_after: A header sent with 429 or 503 that tells the client how many seconds to wait before trying again.
n_sdk: Software Development Kit: a library plus tools that a vendor provides to use its service from code, for example the AWS SDK.
n_seo: Search Engine Optimization: making pages easy for search engines to read and rank. Server-rendered HTML helps because crawlers see the content immediately.
n_sha: The Secure Hash Algorithm family. SHA-256 turns any input into a fixed 256-bit fingerprint. It is fast and one-way, so for passwords use slow hashes (Argon2, bcrypt) instead.
n_sleep: `time.sleep` blocks the whole thread. Inside async code use `await asyncio.sleep(...)`, which lets other tasks run while waiting.
n_slicing: `seq[start:stop:step]` takes a part of a list, tuple or string. `start` is included, `stop` is NOT. Negative indexes count from the end: `s[-1]` is the last item, so `"python"[-1]` is `'n'`.
n_sql_clauses: SQL clauses are evaluated in this logical order: FROM, WHERE (filters rows), GROUP BY, HAVING (filters groups), SELECT (picks columns), ORDER BY, LIMIT.
n_star: Situation, Task, Action, Result: a structure for answering behavioral questions with a short, concrete story.
n_tcp: Transmission Control Protocol: a reliable connection between two machines. It guarantees that data arrives complete and in order. HTTP, databases and SSH run on top of it.
n_testid: An HTML attribute added only for tests, so that a selector stays stable when the styles or the text change.
n_to_thread: Runs a blocking function in a worker thread so that it does not freeze the event loop.
n_token_bucket: A rate limiting algorithm: tokens refill at a steady rate and each request spends one. It allows short bursts (up to the bucket size) while keeping the average rate under control.
n_typevar: A placeholder type used for generic code. `T = TypeVar("T")` lets a function say 'the output has the same type as the input'.
n_udp: A faster, connectionless protocol with no delivery guarantee. Used for video calls, games, DNS lookups and HTTP/3 (through QUIC).
n_useeffect: A React hook for side effects (fetching, subscriptions, timers) that run after render. The dependency array controls when it re-runs; the returned function cleans up.
n_useref: A React hook that keeps a mutable value or a DOM node between renders without causing a re-render.
n_usestate: A React hook that gives a component a piece of state: `const [count, setCount] = useState(0)`. Calling the setter schedules a re-render.
n_uuid: Universally Unique Identifier: a 128-bit random ID like `3f2b8c1e-...`. It can be generated anywhere without coordination, with a negligible chance of collision.
n_vpn: Virtual Private Network: an encrypted tunnel between networks or devices over the internet, so they behave as if they were on the same private network.
n_waf: Web Application Firewall: filters HTTP traffic and blocks common attacks like SQL injection and XSS before they reach the app.
n_war: Web Application Archive: a packaged Java web app that is deployed into a servlet container such as Tomcat. Spring Boot usually builds an executable JAR instead.
n_wip: Work-in-progress limit: a Kanban rule that caps how many items can sit in a column at once, so the team finishes work before it starts more.
n_wraps: A decorator for decorators: it copies the original function's name and docstring onto the wrapper, so debugging and introspection still work.
n_yagni: You Aren't Gonna Need It: do not build a feature until it is really needed.
n_yield: Turns a function into a generator: it pauses and hands back a value, then resumes where it stopped on the next call.
normalization: Organizing tables so each fact is stored once, linked by keys. Avoids duplicate data and update mistakes.
nosql: Databases that are not relational tables: document, key-value, wide-column or graph stores, often with flexible schemas.
null: A marker for 'missing or unknown value' in SQL. It is not 0 or empty string, and comparisons with it are never true (use IS NULL).
o_azure_map: EC2 = VM; S3 = Blob Storage; Lambda = Functions; EKS = AKS; RDS = Azure SQL; DynamoDB = Cosmos DB; IAM = Entra ID + RBAC; CloudWatch = Azure Monitor.
o_azure_rg: A logical container for resources that share a lifecycle. Subscriptions hold resource groups; resource groups hold resources.
o_cicd_tools: Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI and Azure DevOps Pipelines run build, test and deploy steps defined as code.
o_cidr: Writing a network range as address/prefix, e.g. `10.0.1.0/24` = 256 addresses. A smaller prefix number means a bigger network.
o_configmap: A Kubernetes object holding non-sensitive configuration injected into Pods as environment variables or files.
o_crashloop: A Pod state meaning the container keeps crashing and Kubernetes retries with increasing delays.
o_dns_records: A: name to IPv4. AAAA: name to IPv6. CNAME: alias to another name. MX: mail servers. TXT: free text such as verification.
o_docker_cli: Command-line tool: `docker build` (make an image), `run` (start a container), `ps` (list), `logs`, `exec` (shell inside), `stop`, `rm`.
o_ec2: AWS virtual servers (virtual machines) that you configure and manage.
o_ecs_eks: ECS: AWS's container orchestrator. EKS: managed Kubernetes. Fargate: serverless compute for containers, so you manage no nodes.
o_helm: The Kubernetes package manager: charts of templated manifests installed with per-environment values.
o_hybrid: Connecting on-premises networks to the cloud with a site-to-site VPN or a dedicated line (Direct Connect, ExpressRoute).
o_iaas: Infrastructure, Platform and Software as a Service: rented servers; a platform that runs your code; a finished application.
o_ingress: Kubernetes rules that route external HTTP(S) traffic by host and path to Services, implemented by an Ingress Controller.
o_l4_l7: Layer 4 balances raw TCP/UDP connections; layer 7 understands HTTP and can route by URL path or host name.
o_managed_identity: An identity Azure manages for a resource so it can call other services with tokens instead of stored passwords. AWS equivalent: IAM roles.
o_namespace: A logical partition of a cluster (dev, staging, team-a) with its own names, quotas and permissions.
o_nat: Network Address Translation: lets hosts with private IPs reach the internet through a shared public address.
o_private_link: Gives a cloud service a private IP in your network, so traffic never crosses the public internet.
o_pvc: PV: a piece of cluster storage. PVC: a Pod's request for storage; it binds to a PV so data survives Pod restarts.
o_rds_dynamo: RDS: managed relational databases. DynamoDB: serverless NoSQL key-value/document store for massive scale and simple access patterns.
o_registry: A service storing container images for push/pull: Docker Hub, AWS ECR, Azure ACR.
o_resources: Kubernetes CPU/memory settings: requests are reserved for scheduling; limits are the maximum (memory over the limit means OOMKilled).
o_security_group: A virtual firewall attached to a resource: stateful and allow-only (AWS Security Group, Azure NSG). NACLs are stateless subnet-level filters.
o_shared_resp: The provider secures the cloud infrastructure; the customer secures their data, identities, configuration and code.
o_statefulset: StatefulSet: Pods with stable identity and storage (databases). DaemonSet: one Pod per node. Job: a run-to-completion task; CronJob: scheduled Jobs.
o_vpc: A private, isolated virtual network in AWS (VPC) or Azure (VNet), divided into subnets.
o_yaml: A human-readable configuration format based on indentation, used by Kubernetes, Docker Compose, Spring and many CI tools.
oauth: A standard for letting an app get limited access to a user's account on another service without seeing the user's password ('Log in with Google').
object: Any value in Python (a number, a list, a function, a class). Every object has a type, a value and an identity.
object_storage: Storage for files (objects) accessed via an HTTP API, like S3. Very durable and scalable, but not a normal filesystem.
observability: How well you can understand what a running system is doing from its outputs: metrics, logs and traces.
observer: Subscribers register with a subject and are notified automatically when an event happens (publish/subscribe).
ocp: Code should be open for extension (add new behavior) but closed for modification (don't edit tested code to add it).
oom: Out Of Memory killer: a Linux kernel mechanism that kills a process using more memory than allowed.
optimistic_locking: Not locking while reading; when saving, check a version number to detect if someone else changed the row in the meantime.
origin: The combination of scheme, domain and port of a web page, e.g. https://app.example.com:443. Different origin = different site for the browser.
orm: Object-Relational Mapper (Django ORM, SQLAlchemy): lets you work with database rows as Python objects instead of writing SQL by hand.
owasp: A widely used list, published by the OWASP foundation, of the most critical security risks for web applications.
pagination: Returning a large list in smaller pages (e.g. 20 items at a time), using limit/offset or a cursor.
parametrize: A pytest decorator that runs the same test with several sets of inputs.
partition: A failure where parts of a distributed system cannot communicate with each other, while each part keeps running.
password_hashing: Storing a slow, salted, one-way hash of the password (Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt) instead of the password itself.
path_param: A variable part of the URL path that identifies a resource: in `/users/42`, 42 is the user ID.
path_traversal: Using `../` sequences in a file path input to access files outside the intended folder.
pessimistic_locking: Locking rows when you read them (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) so nobody else can change them until you finish.
phishing: Fraudulent messages that impersonate trusted organizations to trick people into giving credentials or installing malware.
pickle: Python's built-in way to convert objects to bytes and back. Used to send data between processes. Never unpickle untrusted data.
pipeline: An automated sequence of steps (lint, test, build, deploy) triggered by code changes.
pod: The smallest unit Kubernetes runs: one or more containers sharing network and storage.
polling: The client repeatedly asks the server 'anything new?' at intervals. Simple but wasteful compared to push.
polymorphism: Different classes respond to the same method call in their own way. The caller just calls `x.area()` without checking the type.
port: A number (0-65535) that identifies a specific service on a machine, e.g. 443 for HTTPS, 5432 for PostgreSQL.
positional_arg: An argument passed by position: `f(10, 20)`. The first value goes to the first parameter, and so on.
postmortem: A written analysis after an incident: what happened, why, and what will change to prevent it.
prefix_sum: An array where each position holds the total of all elements before it, so any range sum is one subtraction.
primary_key: The column(s) that uniquely identify each row in a table. Unique and never NULL.
probe: Health checks Kubernetes runs on Pods: readiness decides if a Pod gets traffic; liveness decides if it must be restarted.
process: A running program with its own private memory. Two processes do not share variables; to exchange data they must send it to each other. Like two separate kitchens.
promise: An object representing the future result of an async operation: pending, then fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error.
property: Turns a method into an attribute you read without parentheses: `circle.area`. Lets you compute or validate values while keeping simple syntax.
property_based: Testing that a rule holds for many automatically generated inputs (e.g. with Hypothesis).
props: Inputs passed from a parent component to a child component. Read-only for the child.
protocol: A type describing required methods. Any class that has those methods matches it, without inheriting from it.
pub_sub: Publish/subscribe messaging: publishers send to a topic; every subscriber of that topic receives a copy.
pytest: The most popular Python testing framework: plain `assert` statements, fixtures, parametrization and plugins.
qps: Queries (requests) per second: a basic measure of load used in capacity estimates.
query_param: Key=value pairs after `?` in a URL, used for filtering, sorting and paging: `?status=paid&limit=10`.
queue: A FIFO collection (first in, first out): add at the back, remove from the front. Like a line of people.
quicksort: A sort that picks a pivot, splits items into smaller and bigger than the pivot, and sorts each part. Fast on average, O(n²) worst case.
race_condition: A bug where the result depends on the unlucky timing of threads or processes touching the same data. Hard to reproduce because it happens only sometimes.
rate_limit: Restricting how many requests a client may make per time window, to protect the service from abuse and overload.
rce: A vulnerability that lets an attacker run their own code on your server. The most severe class of bug.
react: A JavaScript library for building user interfaces from components that re-render when their data changes.
read_replica: A copy of the database that receives changes from the primary and serves read queries.
rebase: Replaying your commits on top of another branch to get a straight-line history. It rewrites commit IDs.
reconciliation: React's process of comparing the new UI description with the previous one and updating only what changed.
recursion: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on smaller inputs, until it reaches a base case.
redis: A very fast in-memory key-value data store, used for caching, counters, sessions, queues and leaderboards.
refactoring: Improving the internal structure of code (names, duplication, organization) without changing its behavior.
reference_counting: CPython counts how many variables or containers point to each object. When the count drops to 0, the object is freed immediately.
regression: A bug where something that used to work stops working after a change. Regression tests guard against it.
replication: Keeping copies of the same data on several servers, for availability and to spread read traffic.
repository: A class that hides how data is stored, offering simple methods like `get`, `add`, `list` to the rest of the code.
repr: `__repr__` gives an exact, developer-oriented description of an object; `__str__` gives friendly text for users. print() uses __str__; lists and the debugger use __repr__.
responsive: Designing pages that adapt their layout to different screen sizes, from phones to desktops.
rest: A popular style for web APIs: URLs name resources (`/users/42`), HTTP methods express actions, and requests are stateless.
retry_backoff: Retrying a failed call after waiting longer each time (1 s, 2 s, 4 s...), with some randomness (jitter) so clients don't retry in sync.
reverse_proxy: A server in front of your app servers that receives client requests and forwards them, often adding TLS, caching and load balancing.
rollback: Returning to the previous working version after a bad release.
routing: Mapping incoming request paths and methods to the functions that handle them.
s3: AWS object storage service for files of any size, organized in buckets.
s_defense_depth: Layering several independent security controls so one failure does not break the whole defense.
s_kms: Managed services that create, store and control encryption keys (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault).
s_sast_dast: SAST scans source code statically; DAST attacks a running app; SCA checks third-party dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
s_sbom: Software Bill of Materials: a list of every component and dependency inside your software, used to find vulnerable libraries quickly.
s_threat_model: A design-time analysis of what can go wrong. STRIDE = Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
salt: A random value added to each password before hashing so that identical passwords produce different hashes.
schema: The structure of the data: which tables or documents exist, their fields, types and relationships.
scope: Where a variable name is visible. Python looks names up in this order: Local (inside the function), Enclosing function, Global (module), Built-in (LEGB).
secret: Sensitive configuration such as passwords, API keys and private keys. Must never be stored in code or logs.
selector: A pattern that chooses which elements a rule applies to: `p` (elements), `.card` (class), `#main` (id), `a:hover` (state).
semantic_html: Using HTML elements for their meaning (button, nav, main, label) instead of generic divs, which helps accessibility and SEO.
semver: Version numbers MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking change, new compatible feature, compatible bug fix.
serverless: Running code without managing servers: the provider runs your function on demand and charges per execution (e.g. AWS Lambda).
service_k8s: A stable network name and IP that load-balances traffic to a changing set of Pods.
session: Server-side memory of a logged-in user, identified by a random session ID usually stored in a cookie.
session_fixation: An attack where the victim is made to log in with a session ID the attacker already knows.
set: An unordered collection of unique values with very fast membership checks: `{1, 2, 3}`.
shallow_copy: A new container that holds the SAME inner objects as the original: `list(a)`, `a.copy()`, `copy.copy(a)`.
sharding: Splitting data across several servers by a key (e.g. user ID), so each holds only part of the data.
signal: A message sent to a process: SIGTERM (15) politely asks it to stop; SIGKILL (9) kills it immediately.
singleton: A class that allows only one instance, reachable from anywhere. Often criticized because it acts like a global variable.
sli_slo_sla: SLI: a measured indicator (e.g. success rate). SLO: the internal target (e.g. 99.9%). SLA: a contractual promise to customers.
sliding_window: A technique that keeps a moving range [left, right] over an array or string, expanding and shrinking it instead of restarting, often O(n).
slots: A class setting that lists the only attribute names its objects may have. It removes the per-object dictionary to save memory.
smoke_test: A small set of quick checks that the most important functions work, typically after a deploy.
solid: Five design principles for maintainable object-oriented code: Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion.
sorting: A method to put items in order. Common ones: merge sort, quicksort, heapsort, Timsort (Python). Good general sorts are O(n log n).
sp_actuator: Adds operational endpoints (health, metrics, info) for monitoring and orchestrator probes.
sp_aop: A technique to apply cross-cutting behavior (logging, security, transactions) around many methods without editing them.
sp_autoconfig: Spring Boot's mechanism to register beans automatically based on the libraries on the classpath and your properties; it backs off when you define your own.
sp_bean: An object created and managed by the Spring container. You get beans by annotating classes (`@Component`, `@Service`) or declaring `@Bean` methods.
sp_bean_scope: How many instances of a bean exist. Default `singleton` (one per container); also `prototype`, `request`, `session`.
sp_bean_validation: Declarative rules on fields (`@NotBlank`, `@Email`, `@Size`) checked when you add `@Valid` to a parameter.
sp_component_scan: Spring searching a package and its sub-packages for stereotype-annotated classes to register as beans.
sp_config_props: Binds groups of properties from `application.yml` to a typed Java class, instead of reading single values with `@Value`.
sp_configuration: A class that declares beans with `@Bean` methods.
sp_constructor_injection: Providing dependencies as constructor parameters. Allows `final` fields, clear requirements and easy unit testing.
sp_controller_advice: A class that applies exception handling (and other advice) to all controllers in one place.
sp_data_jpa: A Spring module that generates repository implementations from interfaces, including queries derived from method names.
sp_dispatcher: Spring MVC's front controller: the single entry point that routes each HTTP request to the right controller method.
sp_dto: A simple class (often a record) shaped for an API request or response, separate from the database entity.
sp_hibernate: The most popular JPA implementation. It generates SQL, manages entity state and caches loaded objects.
sp_ioc: A design where a framework or container controls object creation and wiring instead of your own code calling `new`.
