sp_jackson: The default Java library that converts objects to JSON and JSON to objects.
sp_jakarta: The successor to Java EE. Since Spring Boot 3 the packages are `jakarta.*` instead of `javax.*`.
sp_jdbc: The standard low-level Java API for running SQL on relational databases through drivers.
sp_jpa: The Java standard for mapping objects to relational tables (ORM): `@Entity`, `@Id`, relationships and JPQL queries.
sp_lazy_loading: Loading related data only when it is first accessed. Efficient, but outside a session it throws LazyInitializationException.
sp_path_variable: Binds a part of the URL path to a method parameter: `/users/{id}`.
sp_persistence_context: The set of entities a JPA session currently manages. Changes to them are detected (dirty checking) and written at commit.
sp_profile: A named configuration set (dev, test, prod) activated with `spring.profiles.active`, letting the same app use different settings per environment.
sp_proxy: A wrapper object Spring places around a bean to add behavior (transactions, caching, security). Calls inside the same class bypass it.
sp_request_body: Binds the HTTP request body (JSON) to a Java method parameter.
sp_rest_controller: A controller whose methods return data written straight to the HTTP response body (usually JSON), rather than a view name.
sp_security: The Spring module for authentication, authorization and protection against common attacks (CSRF, session fixation...), built on a chain of servlet filters.
sp_servlet: A servlet is a Java class that handles HTTP requests; a container (Tomcat, Jetty) runs them and manages connections and threads.
sp_spring: A large Java framework for building applications. Its core is a container that creates objects (beans) and wires them together, with modules for web, data, security and testing.
sp_spring_boot: A layer on top of Spring that auto-configures libraries, bundles dependencies into starters and embeds a web server, so apps start with `java -jar`.
sp_starter: A single Maven/Gradle dependency (like `spring-boot-starter-web`) that pulls in a compatible group of libraries for one purpose.
sp_stereotype: `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller` and `@RestController`: markers that register a class as a bean and describe its role.
sp_test_slice: A Spring Boot test annotation that loads only part of the app (`@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`) for fast, focused tests.
sp_transactional: Runs a method inside a database transaction: commit on success, roll back on a RuntimeException by default.
space_complexity: How much extra memory an algorithm needs as the input grows, written in Big-O.
specificity: The weight CSS uses to choose between conflicting rules: inline > id > class > element.
spof: A component without a backup whose failure stops the whole system.
sql: Structured Query Language: the language used to read and change data in relational databases (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE).
sql_injection: An attack where user input is inserted into a SQL query as code, letting the attacker read or change data. Prevented with parameterized queries.
sqs_sns: AWS messaging: SQS is a queue that workers pull from; SNS publishes each message to all subscribers.
srp: A class or module should have one job, so only one kind of change forces you to edit it.
ssh: Secure Shell: an encrypted protocol to log in to and run commands on remote machines.
ssr: Server-side rendering: the server generates the HTML for a page so it arrives already filled with content.
ssrf: Server-Side Request Forgery: making your server send requests to internal or unintended addresses.
stack: A LIFO collection (last in, first out): push adds to the top, pop removes from the top. Like a pile of plates.
staging: A production-like environment used to test releases before they reach real users.
state: Data owned by a component that can change over time; changing it causes a re-render.
stateless: The server keeps no memory of previous requests from a client; each request carries all it needs (e.g. a token).
status_code: A 3-digit number in every HTTP response: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
strategy: Interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, chosen at runtime (e.g. different shipping cost rules).
structural_typing: Type compatibility based on the shape (properties and methods) of a value, not the name of its type.
stub: A test double that returns fixed, pre-programmed answers.
symmetric: Encryption where the same secret key encrypts and decrypts (e.g. AES). Fast.
t_explicit_wait: Waiting until a specific condition is true (element visible, clickable) with a timeout, instead of sleeping a fixed time.
t_junit: The standard Java unit testing framework: `@Test`, `@BeforeEach`, `@ParameterizedTest`, assertions and extensions.
t_locator: The way a test finds an element: by id, name, CSS selector, XPath or link text. Stable locators make tests less brittle.
t_pom: A pattern where each page is a class with its locators and actions, keeping tests readable and UI changes in one place.
t_selenium: A library that controls a real browser from code (open pages, find elements, click, type) to automate UI tests.
table: A set of rows (records) with the same columns (fields), like a spreadsheet with strict column types.
tdd: Writing a failing test first, then just enough code to pass it, then cleaning up: red → green → refactor.
terraform: A popular Infrastructure-as-Code tool that creates and updates cloud resources from configuration files.
test_isolation: Each test sets up and cleans up its own data, so tests don't affect each other and can run in any order.
test_pyramid: Guideline for test mix: many fast unit tests at the bottom, fewer integration tests, very few slow end-to-end tests at the top.
this_js: A keyword whose value depends on how a function is called. Arrow functions take `this` from the surrounding code.
thread: A sequence of instructions running inside a program. One program (process) can have several threads that share the same memory, like several cooks in one kitchen.
throttle: Limiting a function to run at most once per time interval, even if events keep firing (e.g. scrolling).
throughput: How much work a system completes per unit of time, e.g. requests per second.
time_complexity: How the number of steps of an algorithm grows with the input size, usually written in Big-O.
tls: Transport Layer Security: the protocol that encrypts and authenticates network connections. The S in HTTPS.
token: A string a client sends to prove who it is (like a ticket), usually in the `Authorization` header. It replaces sending the password every time.
topological_sort: Ordering the nodes of a DAG so that every node comes after the nodes it depends on.
transaction: A group of database operations treated as one unit: either all succeed (COMMIT) or all are undone (ROLLBACK).
tree: A hierarchical structure of nodes: one root, each node has children, no cycles. Nodes without children are leaves.
trie: A tree where each path from the root spells a prefix; used for autocomplete and prefix searches.
try_except: Syntax to catch errors: code that might fail goes in `try`; the handling code goes in `except SomeError:`. `finally` always runs; `else` runs only if there was no error.
ttl: How long a cached item (or DNS record) stays valid before it expires and must be fetched again.
twelve_factor: A set of 12 practices for cloud-friendly apps, such as config in env vars, stateless processes and logs to stdout.
two_pointers: A technique using two indexes that move through the data (from both ends, or one fast and one slow) to avoid nested loops.
type_hint: Annotations like `def f(x: int) -> str:` that document expected types. Python ignores them at runtime; tools like mypy and editors use them to find bugs.
typescript: JavaScript with static type annotations, checked at compile time and removed when compiled to JS.
union: Combines the results of two SELECT queries into one list. UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them.
union_find: A structure that tracks which elements belong to the same group, with near-O(1) find and union operations.
unique_constraint: A rule that no two rows may have the same value in that column (e.g. email).
unit_test: An automated test of a small piece of code (a function or class) in isolation, with external dependencies replaced by test doubles.
v_bom: A pom that fixes the versions of many libraries so they are compatible and you do not repeat version numbers.
v_branching_strategy: A team's rules for branches: Git Flow (develop/release/hotfix) or trunk-based (frequent merges to main).
v_cherry_pick: Copies the changes of one specific commit onto the current branch as a new commit.
v_dep_scope: Tells Maven when a dependency is needed: compile (default), provided, runtime or test.
v_gav: groupId, artifactId and version: the three values that uniquely identify a Maven artifact.
v_git: A distributed version control system that records the history of your files and supports branches and merging.
v_gitignore: A file listing patterns of files Git should not track, such as build output, IDE settings and secrets.
v_local_repo: The folder `~/.m2/repository` where Maven caches downloaded libraries and stores artifacts from `mvn install`.
v_maven: A Java build and dependency management tool. It reads `pom.xml`, downloads libraries, compiles, tests and packages the project.
v_maven_lifecycle: The ordered phases of a build: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy. Running a phase runs all earlier ones.
v_merge_conflict: Happens when two branches changed the same lines. You must pick the final content manually, then mark it resolved.
v_pom: Project Object Model: the Maven file describing the project (coordinates, dependencies, plugins, properties).
v_pull_request: A request to merge a branch, with code review and automated checks, hosted on GitHub/GitLab (called merge request on GitLab).
v_reflog: A local log of everywhere HEAD has pointed, used to recover "lost" commits after a reset or rebase.
v_remote: A shared copy of the Git repository hosted elsewhere (GitHub, GitLab). `origin` is the default name of the main remote.
v_reset_revert: `reset` moves a branch back and rewrites history; `revert` adds a new commit that undoes an earlier one, safe on shared branches.
v_sdlc: Software Development Life Cycle: the phases from requirements and design through coding, testing, deployment and maintenance.
v_snapshot: A mutable development version (`1.2.0-SNAPSHOT`) that may change, unlike an immutable release version.
v_staging: The waiting area where `git add` places changes you want in the next commit.
v_stash: Temporarily stores uncommitted changes so you can switch tasks and bring them back later.
v_transitive: A library pulled in automatically because one of your dependencies needs it.
validation: Checking that input data has the right shape, types and values before using it. In FastAPI done by Pydantic models.
var_let_const: Ways to declare variables in JS. var: function-scoped and hoisted (old). let: block-scoped, can be reassigned. const: block-scoped, cannot be reassigned.
venv: A self-contained folder with its own Python packages for one project, created with `python -m venv .venv`.
versioning: Labeling API versions (e.g. /v1, /v2) so you can introduce breaking changes without breaking existing clients.
vertical_scaling: Making one server more powerful (more CPU, RAM, disk). Simple but limited and still a single point of failure.
virtual_dom: A lightweight in-memory description of the UI that React compares between renders to compute minimal real DOM changes.
vm: A software emulation of a full computer, running its own operating system on top of a hypervisor.
volume: Storage that lives outside a container's lifecycle, used to keep data such as database files.
web_storage: Browser key-value storage readable by JavaScript. localStorage persists; sessionStorage lasts for one tab.
webhook: An HTTP call that a service makes to YOUR URL when an event happens (e.g. 'payment succeeded'), instead of you asking repeatedly.
websocket: A connection that stays open so server and client can send messages to each other at any time. Used for chat and live updates.
window_function: A function computed over a set of related rows while keeping every row: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, running totals, using OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...).
worker: A process or thread that handles requests or jobs. A server often runs several workers to handle work in parallel.
write_through: Every write goes to both the cache and the database, so the cache is always current.
wsgi_asgi: Standards for how Python web servers run web apps. WSGI is synchronous (Flask, classic Django); ASGI supports async and WebSockets (FastAPI).
xss: An attack where malicious JavaScript gets onto your site and runs in other users' browsers. Prevented by escaping output and CSP.
z_algorithm: A finite, ordered set of steps that solves a problem or performs a task.
z_annotation: A label starting with @ attached to code (`@Override`, `@Service`) that the compiler or a framework reads to change behavior.
z_backend: The part of an application that runs on servers: business logic, database access, security checks and APIs. Users never see it directly.
z_behavioral: Interview questions about how you acted in real past situations. Answer with a structured story such as STAR.
z_bottleneck: The slowest or most limited component, which caps the performance of the whole system.
z_browser: An app (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) that requests web pages from servers and displays them. It is the most common HTTP client.
z_brute_force: Solving a problem by trying every possibility. Simple and correct, but often too slow for large inputs.
z_bug: A bug is a flaw that makes software behave wrongly. Debugging is finding and fixing its cause.
z_cia: The three goals of information security: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability.
z_client_side: Client-side code runs on the user's device (usually the browser). Server-side code runs on a server and answers requests.
z_cloud_provider: Company that rents computing resources over the internet. Largest: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud.
z_code_review: A teammate reads your changes before they are merged, to catch problems and share knowledge.
z_compiler: A program that translates source code into another form, for example Java source into bytecode, or TypeScript into JavaScript.
z_crud: The four basic data operations: Create, Read, Update, Delete (SQL: INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE).
z_data_structure: A way of organizing data in memory so that some operations are efficient: list, dictionary, set, stack, queue, tree, graph.
z_data_type: The kind of value: integer, decimal number, text (string), true/false (boolean), list, dictionary, and so on.
z_database: An organized collection of data stored on disk so programs can search, update and share it safely.
z_dbms: Database Management System: the software that stores the data and runs queries, such as PostgreSQL, MySQL or Oracle Database.
z_deploy: Putting a version of the application on a server or cloud environment so it runs for real users (or testers).
z_devops: A combination of culture, practices and tools that brings development and operations together to deliver software faster and more reliably.
z_entra: Microsoft's cloud identity and access service, formerly Azure Active Directory (Azure AD).
z_field_method: Fields store an object's data (state). Methods are the actions (behavior) the object can perform.
z_firewall: A network control that allows or blocks connections based on rules (address, port, protocol).
z_framework: Reusable foundation of code that gives structure to an application and calls your code at defined points (for example Spring Boot, Django, React).
z_frontend: The part of an application that runs on the user's device (browser or app) and that people see and interact with: layout, buttons, forms.
z_ide: Integrated Development Environment: an editor with extra tools such as autocomplete, a debugger and run/test buttons (IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, PyCharm).
z_indentation: Spaces at the start of a line. In Python they define which lines belong to a block (if, loop, function).
z_interpreter: A program that reads source code and runs it directly. Python code runs with the `python` interpreter.
z_jar: Java ARchive: a ZIP-based file that bundles compiled classes and resources. Libraries and Spring Boot apps are shipped as JARs.
z_java: A general-purpose, object-oriented programming language, very common in backend and enterprise software. Not related to JavaScript.
z_k8s_terms: Cluster: the set of machines managed by Kubernetes. Node: one machine. Pod: smallest deployable unit, running one or more containers.
z_library: A collection of reusable code that your program calls when it needs it (for example requests, Jackson).
z_linux: Free, open source operating system family that runs most servers, containers and cloud machines.
z_loop: A structure that repeats a block of code, for example `for` (once per item) or `while` (as long as a condition is true).
z_lts: A release that receives updates and fixes for several years. Java 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25 are LTS versions.
z_malware: Malicious software: viruses, worms, ransomware, spyware and other programs designed to harm or steal.
z_manual_vs_auto: Manual: a person runs the steps and judges the result. Automated: code runs the checks quickly and repeatedly.
z_markup: A language that labels content with tags to describe its structure or meaning, such as HTML. It is not a programming language: it has no logic.
z_module: A module is a file of code you can import; a package is a folder of modules.
z_monitoring: Watching metrics (errors, latency, CPU) over time and alerting when the system is unhealthy.
z_mvp: Minimum Viable Product: the smallest version of a product that delivers value and lets the team learn from real users.
z_nist_cloud: On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service.
z_nodejs: A JavaScript runtime that lets you run JavaScript outside the browser, for example to build servers and command-line tools.
z_null_java: The value of a reference that points to no object. Calling a method on it throws NullPointerException.
z_object_storage: Storage for whole files (objects) accessed by key or URL, like Amazon S3 and Azure Blob Storage. Not a database.
z_oop: Object-oriented programming: organizing code into objects that bundle data (fields) and behavior (methods).
z_package: A namespace that organizes related classes and interfaces, like a folder: `java.util`, `com.mycompany.shop`.
z_package_manager: A tool that downloads and tracks the libraries a project needs: Maven or Gradle (Java), pip (Python), npm (JavaScript).
z_parameter: A parameter is a variable in a function's definition (`def greet(name)`). An argument is the value you pass when calling it (`greet("Ana")`).
z_patch: An update that fixes a bug or a security vulnerability in software.
z_persistence: Keeping data after the program stops, by saving it on disk (for example in a database) instead of only in memory.
z_pii: Personally Identifiable Information: data that can identify a person, such as name, email, ID number or address.
z_pip: Python's package installer. It downloads packages from PyPI (the Python Package Index).
z_programming_language: A formal language for writing instructions that a computer can execute, such as Python, Java or JavaScript.
z_qa: Quality Assurance: activities (testing, automation, process improvements) that help make sure software meets quality expectations.
z_query: A request written for a database to get or change data, usually in SQL.
z_region_az: A Region is a geographic area; an Availability Zone is an isolated data center location inside it. Spread across AZs for high availability.
z_server: A computer or a program that waits for requests from clients and sends back responses.
z_stack: The set of technologies used to build an application: for example React + Spring Boot + PostgreSQL.
z_stakeholder: Anyone affected by or interested in a project: users, customers, managers, other teams.
z_static_dynamic: Static: the server sends the same ready-made files to everyone. Dynamic: the server builds the page for each request, usually with data from a database.
z_system_design: Deciding the main components of a system and how they work together to meet requirements for scale, reliability and speed.
z_tech_debt: The future cost of quick or messy solutions taken now. It slows later changes until it is repaid.
z_terminal: The terminal is the text window; the shell (Bash, Zsh, PowerShell) interprets the commands you type.
z_test_case: A test case checks one scenario against an expected result. A suite is a group of test cases run together.
z_ticket: A tracked unit of work (bug, task, story) in a tool such as Jira, with owner, status and priority.
z_trade_off: A choice where improving one quality (speed) costs another (simplicity, consistency, money).
z_ui_ux: UI (user interface) is what the user sees and uses. UX (user experience) is the whole experience of using the product.
z_url: Uniform Resource Locator: the address of a resource, made of scheme (https), host (example.com), optional port, path (/products) and query (?id=7).
z_variable: A name that refers to a value stored in memory, so the value can be used or changed later.
z_vulnerability: A weakness in software, configuration or process that an attacker could exploit.
